transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Pierce (Redwood AE); Riya Patel (Redwood SE); Miguel Alvarez (CatalystHealth CTO); Laura Chen (Head of MLOps); Samir Patel (Security Lead)

Summary: Discovery focused on Dedicated capacity for PHI-containing workloads. Customer exploring dedicated GPUs for production inferencing with isolation (VPC/on-prem considerations), burst strategy for peak traffic, and predictable scaling. Security questions around KMS, audit logs, SSO, and data residency. Discussed pilot scope and benchmark plan.

Topics: dedicated capacity sizing, burst capacity, autoscaling policies, private deployment vs hosted fallbacks, SOC2/KMS/audit logs, cost vs latency tradeoffs, next steps for pilot.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Pierce: Hey everyone, thanks for taking time. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Riya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Miguel Alvarez: Doing well thanks. We're excited to talk through the Dedicated options, Miguel here.
[00:12] Laura Chen: Hi all, Laura—ML infra. We're evaluating because we have PHI use cases and worried about co-tenancy and latencies.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Samir from security—quick hits: encryption at rest, KMS integration, audit logs, SSO.
[00:23] Riya Patel: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: we want to understand your workload (QPS, seq lengths), isolation requirements, acceptable latencies, and timeline for pilot/rollout. We'll also cover burst patterns and autoscaling.
[00:33] Miguel Alvarez: Sounds good. To start, high level: we're running a conversational triage assistant for urgent care; it touches PHI so we need isolation. Peak traffic currently is spiky—5 to 6k QPS for short bursts during clinics, baseline about 300 QPS. Token lengths average 400 tokens per request, sometimes up to 1k. Latency SLO 200-300ms tail for user-facing responses.
[00:50] Riya Patel: Got it. Two parts—capacity for sustained baseline and then burst pool. For Dedicated we usually size a reserved GPU pool for your baseline throughput and provide burst capacity using pre-reserved spare nodes or configured burst credits. We can also do automatic fallback to our hosted fleet if you want extra headroom.
[01:08] Laura Chen: Fallback to hosted raises concerns about data residency and PHI leaving the VPC. Is that a hard no for the team?
[01:14] Samir Patel: Yes, we need all PHI to remain within our controlled environment. We can explore Private (VPC) deployment rather than a hosted fallback.
[01:20] Jordan Pierce: Understood. Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) is an option—same API surface, private control plane. For Dedicated reserved pools in a VPC we can guarantee isolation and keep KV cache and any logs inside your network.
[01:33] Miguel Alvarez: Our preference is Dedicated inside our VPC; we might consider a hybrid where non-PHI traffic uses hosted. But for the pilot, PHI must stay private.
[01:40] Riya Patel: Perfect. For sizing: with your avg 400 tokens and 300 baseline QPS, rough estimates indicate X GPUs for baseline—I'm going to explain with some ballpark numbers: with current gen A100-equivalent nodes and our optimized runtime, one node could handle roughly 250-350 QPS at 400 tokens depending on batching. So baseline of 300 suggests 1-2 nodes reserved, with burst policy to scale to ~6k QPS using burst pool or additional reserved capacity.
[02:08] Laura Chen: That variability is big. Can you run a benchmark using our prompt set? We need deterministic numbers.
[02:13] Riya Patel: Absolutely. We'll run an on-prem benchmark or Remote benchmark in your VPC. We'll need your sample prompts and token distribution. We'll instrument tail latency, p50/p95/p99, and cost per 1k tokens.
[02:25] Miguel Alvarez: Timeline? We want results before end of year. Can that happen?
[02:29] Jordan Pierce: Yes—if you share artifacts this week we can run a 5-day pilot/bench and share results next week.
[02:35] Samir Patel: Security—what about KMS? We use AWS KMS and HSM for key management. Does Redwood integrate with customer-managed KMS?
[02:42] Riya Patel: We support customer-managed KMS and HSM options for Private deployments; for Dedicated in-cloud we integrate with your cloud KMS via our private control plane. We can provide key wrapping and ensure model artifacts are encrypted at rest with your keys.
[02:55] Samir Patel: And audit logs? Need immutable audit trails for inference events and admin actions.
[03:00] Jordan Pierce: We have sys-level audit logs and SSO/SAML integrations; for Private deployments logs can be delivered to your SIEM. We'll share SOC 2 docs and logging architecture.
[03:10] Laura Chen: On scaling, how does autoscaling work for Dedicated? Will warm KV caches cause cold start spikes?
[03:17] Riya Patel: Good question. Our runtime manages KV cache and continuous batching. We recommend keeping a minimum pool to avoid cold-start latency for user-facing SLOs. For bursts, we offer warm standby nodes and a burst queue; when load exceeds headroom we can spin up additional nodes—time-to-scale typically in the 20-90s range depending on model size and init steps. We also support cache pre-warming and snapshot restores to reduce cold startup.
[03:38] Miguel Alvarez: 20-90s could be too long for some flows. Can you provision a burst buffer to hit our 200ms p99 target?
[03:45] Riya Patel: For sub-300ms tails at 400 tokens you'll need dedicated nodes reserved for peak or very aggressive warm standby. Often customers commit to a baseline reserved capacity for predictable percent of traffic and rely on burst credits for infrequent spikes. We'll show cost tradeoffs in the pricing options.
[03:59] Jordan Pierce: We can propose a hybrid commit: reserved capacity sized for 70% of your peak plus a burst pool and fallback model variants (smaller quantized models) for emergency high load. That preserves a p99 for most traffic and reduces cost.
[04:12] Samir Patel: Tell me more about model variants and quantization—does Redwood handle that or do we manage model conversions?
[04:18] Riya Patel: Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles and we can host quantized variants. We handle kernel selection and execution paths in the runtime. For private deployments there is a model onboarding step where we validate the quantized variant and provide perf profiles.
[04:31] Laura Chen: Network topologies—we need traffic to stay inside our VPC. How does egress to Redwood control plane happen?
[04:37] Jordan Pierce: For Private, control plane can be customer-hosted or run in a private peered region. All telemetry and control messages can be routed over peered links; sensitive logs and data flows can be disabled or delivered to your logging endpoints. We'll supply architecture diagrams.
[04:51] Miguel Alvarez: Any limitations on model sizes for Dedicated? We're evaluating open LLMs at ranging sizes—up to 70B parameters.
[04:58] Riya Patel: We support large models and have optimized paths for various sizes; bigger models may require multi-GPU sharding which impacts cold start and scaling times. We'll include model-specific perf numbers in the benchmark.
[05:09] Samir Patel: Compliance: we need SOC2 Type II and an ISO roadmap. Do you provide these artifacts?
[05:15] Jordan Pierce: Yes. We'll send SOC 2 report and our security posture doc. If you need a specific compliance add-on (e.g., added retention controls), we can scope that in the contract.
[05:24] Laura Chen: Procurement question: what are committed terms and options? Monthly, annual? Can we do a 6-month pilot commit?
[05:30] Jordan Pierce: Typical Reserved Dedicated is monthly or annual commitments. For pilots we often do a time-limited reserved pool with a cap and a conversion path to annual commits. We'll include a 6-month pilot option in the proposal.
[05:39] Miguel Alvarez: Costs are a big factor. We want per-token cost and per-GPU hour nondiscounted. Also how you charge for burst usage.
[05:46] Riya Patel: We'll provide a pricing sheet: baseline reserved unit pricing, burst credits pricing, and on-demand fallback. We'll show example math for your 400-token avg workload.
[05:55] Samir Patel: One more technical: auditability of model outputs—retention of logs and ability to pull transcripts for audits.
[06:01] Jordan Pierce: You can set retention and routing rules; for Private we can keep transcripts in your S3 or SIEM. We can also redaction hooks if needed.
[06:09] Laura Chen: Great. For the pilot we want to validate latency and cost and run regression tests on hallucination rates across two model variants.
[06:17] Riya Patel: We'll run evals and include quality metrics and regression alerts. Please attach prompt sets and expected ground truth.
[06:24] Miguel Alvarez: Ok action items then?
[06:27] Jordan Pierce: I'll recap: Jordan to send pricing and commit options; Riya to share benchmark template and onboarding checklist; you to provide sample prompts, traffic profiles, and any compliance questions; Samir to confirm KMS/HSM specifics. We'll schedule the pilot kickoff once artifacts are in.
[06:43] Laura Chen: Sounds good. Any open concerns?
[06:46] Samir Patel: We want written confirmation that PHI won't leave our VPC for the pilot—can you include that in the security note?
[06:52] Jordan Pierce: Yes, we'll include language for the pilot environment and scope in the security doc.
[06:56] Miguel Alvarez: Thanks all.
[06:58] Jordan Pierce: Thanks, we'll follow up with the docs and pricing by Thursday.

Endnotes: A few miss-transcriptions in the automated text: sometimes "KV cache" appears as "KB cache" and product names (e.g., Redwood Dedicated) were occasionally split. This recording is medium quality transcription; manual review recommended before feeding to CRM.
